item.title: Dolly Parton told us who she was, one song at a time
item.description:
My introduction to Dolly Parton came at 7. My mom, as the lead alto in the church choir, had some sway with our music director and she used it to snag me the occasional solo in front of the congregation. I sang hymns, some contemporary Christian songs. Then one day, Mom brought home the sheet music for “Coat of Many Colors.” The song wasn’t in the Baptist hymnal, but she seemed confident it would pass muster (after all, who doesn’t love Dolly?). I practiced at home, committing the lyrics to heart. I took my position on stage by the pulpit one Sunday, facing pews stuffed with people, and scanned the crowd for my mom as I started to sing. For the first time during one of my performances, she wept. My mom drew the parallels between Parton’s song and her own life — she, too, had grown up as an impoverished kid from a big family, and she’d learned a little bit about turning humble beginnings…

item.title: How Parton became a fashion icon
item.description:
Dolly Parton, the country music legend behind hits like “Jolene” and “9 to 5,” as well as an actress, businesswoman, fashion icon , and philanthropist , died on Tuesday. She was 80. Her death was announced in a video featuring her nephew, Bryan Seaver, that was shared on Parton’s social media accounts. Seaver didn’t disclose a cause of death in the video, but Parton’s publicist later told news outlets in a statement that Parton died after a “brief battle with cancer.” In the video, Seaver said that his aunt “has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by” her loved ones, including her husband Carl Dean, who died last year , as well as her parents and “countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens.” “She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history,” Seaver said. “My family and I have…

item.title: Why Trump’s plan to rescind the Roadless Rule protecting national forests will struggle in court
item.description:
Roadless areas in Alaska contain important old-growth forests. Mike Reid Photography/Moment via Getty Images Over 368,000 miles of roads wind through U.S. national forests, eight times more than the entire interstate highway system . Many are heavily eroded and prone to landslides, and driving vehicles on them can spread invasive species. They need billions of dollars in repairs. Yet the Trump administration wants to build more roads in America’s national forests to expand timber production, specifically in untouched areas currently protected by the 2001 federal Roadless Rule . In announcing the administration’s formal proposal to rescind the Roadless Area Conservation Rule on Aug. 18, 2026, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins argued that building roads in these areas is important for fighting wildfires. However, data show that roads actually tend to increase the risk of fires…

item.title: Data Center Developers in Texas Plan Massive New Gas Power Projects
item.description:
The capacity of gas-fired power plants currently being planned to supply power to US data centers nearly doubled in the first half of 2026. A new study from Global Energy Monitor counted 189 gigawatts of gas-fired capacity in development in the first half of 2026. But it remains unclear if all of those plants will ultimately be built, since most projects are in early development and the demand surge has led to a bottleneck for gas turbines, with some suppliers warning of yearslong lead times. The buildout could also be affected by the growing political backlash to data centers, which is increasingly bipartisan . A Heatmap poll showed 75% of US voters oppose new data centers in their area. Texas — which the report highlights is the epicenter of the gas boom — has recently backtracked on its welcoming stance towards data centers and passed a moratorium on new projects. — Eugenia Perozo
